```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%", dev = "svglite",
  fig.ext = "svg", dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A")
```

A vector field assigns a direction and magnitude to each position in space.
This article draws arrows at sampled positions, then integrates curves through
the field and gives those curves thickness. Installation is covered in
[Get started](ggplot3d.html).

1. **Map** the position and vector components with `geom_quiver_3d()`.

2. **Trace** curves through a regular grid with `stat_streamline_3d()`.

3. **Thicken** the curves by choosing the tube geometry.

## Example

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA)))
```

The example field rotates around the z axis and rises at a constant rate.
Its components are u = -y, v = x and w = 0.2. Sample it on a complete grid
with five positions on each horizontal axis and three heights. Every x/y/z
combination appears once; a missing component value stops a curve when it
reaches the affected cells.

```{r field}
field <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 5),
                     y = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 5), z = c(-1, 0, 1))
field$u <- -field$y
field$v <- field$x
field$w <- 0.2
head(field, 3)
```

### Arrows and cones

Each arrow starts at its mapped position and follows its three components.
The length multiplier controls how much of the field is covered by one
arrow. Draw a subset of the grid to leave room between arrows; the full
grid will supply the streamline integration.

```{r quiver, fig.alt="Solid-headed arrows rotating around z and pointing slightly upward, coloured by vector magnitude."}
arrows <- subset(field, x %in% c(-1, 0, 1) & y %in% c(-1, 0, 1) & z != 0)
vectors <- ggplot(arrows, aes(x, y, z = z, u = u, v = v, w = w))
vectors + geom_quiver_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(norm)), scale = 0.4,
                         shaft = "tube", detail = 0) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = PAL["blue"], name = "magnitude") +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

The computed magnitude remains available when arrows are normalised.
Normalisation sets each input vector to unit length before the length
multiplier is applied. A middle pivot centres the arrow on its anchor;
tail and tip pivots attach the corresponding end.

```{r normalized, fig.alt="Equal-length arrows centred on their anchors, with colour retaining the original vector magnitude."}
vectors + geom_quiver_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(norm)), scale = 0.5,
  normalize = TRUE, pivot = "middle", detail = 0) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = PAL["blue"], name = "magnitude") +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

Cones use the same anchors and components, with each vector drawn as one
solid cone. Their orientation follows the scale transformations and the
aspect ratio. Zero-length vectors produce no geometry.

```{r cones, fig.alt="Cones representing the rotating field, with their size and fill following vector magnitude."}
vectors + geom_cone_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(norm)), scale = 0.5, detail = 0) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF3", high = PAL["orange"], name = "magnitude") +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

### Streamlines from seed points

A streamline follows the field from a starting position, called a seed.
Choose three seeds at different distances from the rotation axis. Trilinear
interpolation supplies components between grid positions, and the adaptive
Runge-Kutta integrator traces each curve forward through the field.

```{r streamlines, fig.alt="Three rising helical streamlines starting at different radii, coloured by their distance travelled."}
flow <- ggplot(field, aes(x, y, z = z, u = u, v = v, w = w))
seeds <- rbind(c(0.3, 0, -0.8), c(0.55, 0, -0.8), c(0.8, 0, -0.8))
lines <- flow + stat_streamline_3d(aes(colour = after_stat(arclength)),
  seeds = seeds, method = "rk45", direction = "forward",
  step = 0.08, max_steps = 90, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = PAL["blue"], high = PAL["orange"],
                         name = "distance") + coord_3d(aspect = "data")
lines
```

The stat exposes magnitude, step index, distance travelled and integration
time. Distance accumulates along each output curve. Integration time is the
parameter in the equation dp/dt = v(p); it has a physical time unit when
the component units are distance per unit time.

```{r computed}
trace <- layer_data(lines)
head(trace[c("x", "y", "z", "norm", "step", "arclength", "time")], 3)
```

Choose the fixed-step RK4 method for a fixed integration step. The adaptive
RK45 method controls local error through its tolerance argument. The step
argument sets the maximum time increment; speed determines the distance
travelled in that increment. Both methods stop at the grid boundary, a
missing field cell, zero speed or the step limit.

### Seed rakes and planes

A rake distributes seeds along a line between two endpoints. Here four
seeds start at increasing radii, all at the same height. A plane
specification instead distributes seeds over the chosen coordinate plane.

```{r rake, fig.alt="Four rising streamlines traced from evenly spaced seeds along a radial line."}
flow + stat_streamline_3d(
  seeds = list(from = c(0.25, 0, -0.8), to = c(0.85, 0, -0.8), n = 4),
  direction = "forward", step = 0.08, max_steps = 70,
  colour = PAL["blue"], linewidth = 0.8) + coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

For example, `list(plane = "xz", at = 0, n = c(3, 2))` seeds an x/z
plane at y = 0. Explicit seeds and plane positions use original position
units. Integration runs in transformed coordinates, so components for a
nonlinear position scale must use its transformed units.

### Streamtubes

The tube geometry sweeps a circular cross-section along each integrated
curve. Radius uses transformed data units and sides controls the circular
resolution. Here three tubes follow the same seeds as the line example.

```{r streamtubes, fig.alt="Three solid helical streamtubes rising around z, coloured by the field magnitude."}
flow + stat_streamline_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(norm)), geom = "tube",
  seeds = seeds, direction = "forward", step = 0.1, max_steps = 60,
  radius = 0.025, sides = 6, cap = "flat", colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = PAL["blue"], high = PAL["orange"],
                       name = "magnitude") + coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

Tube faces retain the mean computed values of their corners. The
[Layers](layers.html#tubes-ribbons-and-sweeps) article shows tube radii,
ribbons and custom cross-sections on supplied paths.

### Evenly spaced curves in a slice

Even spacing traces the field projected into each requested slice. Change
the horizontal components to a flow along x with a sideways component
proportional to x. In the x/y plane the vertical component is set to zero,
so the output stays at the selected height.

Seed spacing controls the separation of candidate curves. The testing
distance stops tracing as a curve approaches an accepted one.

```{r even-slices, fig.alt="Evenly spaced curved streamlines projected into two horizontal slices of a sheared flow."}
shear <- transform(field, u = 1, v = 0.4 * x)
ggplot(shear, aes(x, y, z = z, u = u, v = v, w = w)) + stat_streamline_3d(
  seeds = list(type = "even", plane = "xy", at = c(-0.5, 0.5),
               spacing = 0.35, dtest = 0.15),
  max_steps = 100, max_lines = 12, colour = PAL["teal"], linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

Automatic even seeding can produce no curves when the slice centre has
zero projected speed, as in the rotating field above. Use explicit seed
points to trace that field away from its stationary centre.
